stages.title: LLM Fundamentals + RAG
stages.description: Tokens, context windows, function calling, chunking and retrieval.
stages.overview: Before you can change how a model behaves you need to be fluent in using one as it is. This stage is the same ground the AI Engineer path covers first: what a model does, how to prompt it reliably, and how to feed it your own documents through retrieval. Work through it properly, because stage 2 is largely about deciding when these techniques are not enough.

topics.definition: A large language model is a program that predicts the next piece of text given the text before it. It has been trained on an enormous amount of writing, which makes those predictions useful for answering questions, summarising and writing code. It does not look anything up and it does not reason about truth; it produces the continuation its training makes most likely. Everything it does well and everything it gets wrong follows from that single behaviour.

Models do not read characters or words, they read tokens — short chunks of text, roughly three to four characters each. A common word is usually one token, while a rare name might be four or five. This matters in practice because you are billed per token, context limits are counted in tokens, and response time scales with how many the model has to produce.

The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, counting your input and its reply together. Anything outside it does not exist as far as the model is concerned. When a conversation or a document grows past that limit you have to summarise, truncate, or retrieve only the relevant parts — which is what the next stage is about.

The system prompt holds standing instructions: what role the model is playing, what format to use, what it must refuse. The user prompt is the specific request. Keeping them apart means you can change the request without restating the rules every time, and models are trained to give system instructions more weight.

Models follow literal instructions far better than implied ones. State what output you want, in what format, and what to do at the edges, rather than trusting the model to infer it. A surprising share of “the model is bad at this” turns out to be a prompt that never said what “this” meant.

Telling the model to answer as a particular kind of expert shifts its vocabulary, level of detail and default assumptions. It is a cheap way to set register and depth for an audience. It does not give the model knowledge it lacks — it only changes how it draws on what it already has.

Rather than describing the output you want, show two or three worked examples in the prompt and let the model infer the pattern. For anything with a consistent shape — classification labels, a particular formatting style — this is usually more reliable than a written description. Choose examples that cover the awkward cases, not just the obvious ones.

Asking for a specific shape — a bullet list, a table, JSON — makes a response easier for both people and code to use. Be explicit about the exact headings or keys you expect rather than describing them loosely. Format instructions placed in the system prompt tend to hold up better across a long conversation.

Structured outputs make the model return data conforming to a schema you supply, so you get valid JSON rather than JSON wrapped in an apology. The provider enforces the shape instead of you parsing and hoping. Use it any time the response feeds code rather than a person.

Tool calling lets you describe functions the model may invoke — search a database, fetch a price, send an email. The model does not run them: it returns the name and arguments it wants, your code executes it, and you pass the result back. This is the mechanism that turns a text generator into something that can act, and stage 3 is built entirely on it.

Temperature controls how much randomness goes into choosing each next token. Low values give consistent, repeatable text; higher values give more variety. For extraction, classification, or anything you intend to parse, keep it near zero — there is no setting that makes the model more correct, only less predictable.

A hallucination is output that is stated confidently and is simply wrong — an invented citation, a function that does not exist. It happens because the model generates plausible continuations, and plausible is not the same as true. You reduce it by supplying the facts in the prompt, asking for sources, and verifying anything that matters; you do not eliminate it.

Instead of one prompt doing five things, break the work into steps and feed each result into the next. Every step becomes easier to test, cheaper to retry and far easier to debug when the output is wrong. It is the simplest version of the multi-step pattern you meet again with agents.

A template is a prompt with typed slots — the user's question, the retrieved documents, today's date — filled in at runtime. Keeping templates in version control rather than scattered through the code means changes get reviewed and can be rolled back. Treat prompts as source code, because that is what they are.

Judging a prompt by trying it once is how bad prompts reach production. Keep a small set of representative inputs with known good answers and re-run them whenever you change the wording. This is a manual habit at this stage and becomes automated testing in stage 6.

An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers that represents its meaning. Texts about similar things end up with similar numbers even when they share no words at all. That property is what makes it possible to search by meaning rather than by matching characters.

Keyword search fails whenever the user's words differ from the document's — “how do I cancel” against a page titled “ending your subscription”. Comparing embeddings compares meaning, so that match succeeds. This is what lets you retrieve the right passage without having anticipated the exact phrasing.

Embeddings are produced by their own models, separate from the ones that generate text. Each produces vectors of a fixed size, and vectors from different models are not comparable with one another. Pick one deliberately, because changing it later means re-embedding everything you have stored.

Once text is embedded, finding related content becomes arithmetic: which stored vectors sit closest to the query vector. Closeness is normally cosine similarity, which compares direction rather than distance. What comes back is a ranked list of candidates, not a single correct answer.

Semantic search is the whole pipeline: embed the query, find the nearest stored vectors, return the original text. It is the retrieval half of RAG and a useful feature in its own right. Its quality depends far more on how you split the documents than on which embedding model you picked.

A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly. Comparing against every vector is fine for a few thousand and hopeless for millions, so these use approximate indexes that trade a little accuracy for a large speed gain. Qdrant, Pinecone and pgvector inside Postgres are all common choices.

“Vector store” is the framework-level abstraction over whichever database you chose — the same add, search and delete calls whether the backend is Qdrant, Pinecone or a local file. Writing against it keeps your application from being welded to one vendor. Start with the simplest option that works and swap later if you need to.

Alongside each vector you can store ordinary fields — author, date, customer id, document type — and restrict a search to matching records. This is how you stop one customer retrieving another's documents, and how you keep answers to current policy rather than last year's. Decide on these fields before you index, because adding them afterwards means re-indexing.

Documents are too long to embed whole, so they get split into passages. Chunks that are too large dilute the meaning and waste context; chunks that are too small lose the surrounding sense. A few hundred tokens with a little overlap is a reasonable starting point, and tuning this improves retrieval more than almost anything else you can change.

The retrieval pipeline is the full path from raw file to prompt-ready text: load, clean, chunk, embed, store, then at query time embed and search. Each stage quietly degrades the next — a poor PDF extraction produces poor chunks, which produce poor matches. Inspect the intermediate output, not only the final answer.

Retrieval-augmented generation means finding relevant text first and including it in the prompt, so the model answers from your documents rather than from memory. It addresses two problems at once: the model not knowing your data, and the model inventing answers when it does not. The model still writes the reply — you are controlling what it has to work from.

The minimal loop is four steps: take the question, retrieve the top few matching chunks, put them in the prompt with an instruction to answer only from them, return the result. Everything more elaborate is a refinement of those four. Build this version first and measure it before adding anything on top.

RAG changes what the model knows; fine-tuning changes how it behaves. If the answer lives in documents that change, retrieve them. If you need a consistent tone, format or task-specific skill, fine-tune. Reaching for fine-tuning to teach facts is the common and expensive mistake.

Semantic search misses exact strings — part numbers, error codes, surnames — because those carry little meaning to embed. Hybrid retrieval runs keyword search alongside vector search and merges the results. It is the usual fix when retrieval looks fine in testing and falls over on real queries containing identifiers.

Instead of retrieving once and answering, the model decides whether to search, judges whether the results are good enough, and searches again with a better query. This handles questions that need several lookups to answer. It costs more calls and more time, so use it where one-shot retrieval demonstrably falls short.

A RAG system can fail at retrieval or at generation, and the two have to be measured separately. Ask first whether the right passages were found, then whether the answer actually followed them. Without a fixed test set you are guessing, and changes that feel like improvements frequently are not.

stages.title: Fine-Tuning (LoRA/QLoRA)
stages.description: When to fine-tune vs RAG, dataset curation.
stages.overview: Fine-tuning continues training an existing model on your own examples, so it learns a behaviour rather than being told about one each time. This is the first stage in any path where you train something, and the first question is always whether you should — retrieval solves more problems, more cheaply. The techniques here make it affordable enough that the answer is sometimes yes.

topics.definition: RAG changes what the model knows; fine-tuning changes how it behaves. If the answer lives in documents that change, retrieve them. If you need a consistent tone, format or task-specific skill, fine-tune. Reaching for fine-tuning to teach facts is the common and expensive mistake.

Fully retraining a model means updating billions of parameters, which needs hardware most teams do not have. LoRA freezes the original model and trains a small set of extra weights alongside it, capturing the new behaviour in a file that is megabytes rather than gigabytes. QLoRA goes further by compressing the frozen model first, which is what brings fine-tuning within reach of a single ordinary GPU.

Fine-tuning quality is set almost entirely by the examples you feed it, and a few hundred consistent ones beat tens of thousands of noisy ones. Remove duplicates, because repeated examples get weighted more heavily and skew the result. Hold some examples back before you start, or you have nothing honest to measure against afterwards.

A fine-tuned model must be compared with the model you started from, on the same inputs. Without that comparison you cannot tell whether it improved, or whether it simply got better at your training examples while getting worse at everything else. Expect some of that trade — the question is whether it is worth it.

Quantisation stores a model's numbers at lower precision, cutting memory and cost at some expense of quality. The loss is often small enough not to matter and occasionally large enough to break a specific task. Measure it on your own workload rather than trusting a general claim, because where the damage lands varies by model and by task.

stages.title: Multimodal AI
stages.description: Vision models, image generation basics, audio.
stages.overview: Not everything is text. This stage covers models that read images, generate them, and handle speech, plus how they differ from the language models you have used so far. The interfaces are similar enough to feel familiar and the failure modes are not, which is the main thing to take from it.

topics.definition: Diffusion models generate an image by starting from random noise and removing a little of it at a time, guided by your prompt, until a picture is left. This is a different mechanism from the next-token prediction behind language models. It explains why image generation takes many steps, why step count trades speed against quality, and why the same prompt twice gives different pictures.

A vision-language model accepts images alongside text, so you can pass a screenshot, a diagram or a photograph and ask questions about it. In practice it works like the models you already use, with images as another kind of input. They read text in images reasonably well and count, measure and reason spatially considerably worse.

Producing usable images is rarely one call: it is a prompt, a negative prompt, a size and step count, often a seed for repeatability, and frequently a second pass to upscale or repair. Wiring those into a repeatable pipeline is what separates a demo from a feature. Store the parameters alongside each output, or you will not be able to reproduce the good ones.

Speech-to-text turns recordings into text, text-to-speech does the reverse, and both are now accurate enough for production use. They pair naturally with the language models you already know — transcribe, process the text, optionally speak the answer. Accuracy drops sharply with background noise, strong accents and specialist vocabulary, so test on real recordings.

stages.title: Evaluation for Generative Systems
stages.overview: Generated output rarely has one correct answer, so ordinary testing does not apply — you cannot assert equality against a picture or a paragraph. This stage covers judging quality at scale: fixed test sets, using a model as a grader, and where human judgement is still the only option. Without this you are shipping changes on the basis of a few examples that felt better.

topics.definition: A RAG system can fail at retrieval or at generation, and the two have to be measured separately. Ask first whether the right passages were found, then whether the answer actually followed them. Without a fixed test set you are guessing, and changes that feel like improvements frequently are not.

Using a model to grade another model's output scales in a way that human review cannot. It also inherits biases worth knowing about: judges tend to prefer longer answers, favour text from the same model family, and are swayed by the order in which options are presented. Give the judge an explicit rubric, randomise the order, and check its verdicts against human ones periodically.

A golden set is a fixed collection of inputs with agreed-good outputs, kept under version control and re-run on every change. It is what turns a subjective impression into a comparison. Include the awkward cases and the past failures, because a test set of easy examples will tell you everything is fine.

For anything where taste matters, the reliable measure is showing people two outputs and asking which is better. Pairwise comparison is far more consistent than asking someone to score a single output out of ten. It is slow and expensive, so use it to validate your automated measures rather than as the everyday check.

stages.title: Deployment & Monitoring
stages.overview: Everything so far has run on your machine or in a notebook. This stage is about getting it onto a server, keeping it running, and being able to say what happened when it misbehaves. Most of it is ordinary backend practice rather than anything specific to generative models, which is exactly why it is worth learning properly.

topics.definition: Development servers reload on save, print stack traces and trust their surroundings; production servers must be secure, restart on failure and give nothing away to an attacker. The gap between the two is where most first deployments break. Assume that nothing which worked locally is configured on the server.

Docker packages your application together with its dependencies into an image that runs identically anywhere. It removes the entire class of failure where code works on your machine but not on the server. For AI work, where Python and native library versions are unusually brittle, this matters more than it does for most software.

A Dockerfile is the recipe for an image: the base, the dependencies, your code, and the command that starts it. Order the steps so the parts that rarely change come first, because Docker caches by layer and rebuilds everything after the first thing that changed. Never bake secrets into it.

Compose runs several containers together from one file — your API, a database, a vector store — with the networking between them handled for you. It is how you reproduce a realistic environment on your own machine. For a single service it is unnecessary; for anything with a datastore it saves a great deal of setup.

Getting a service live means a process manager that restarts it, a reverse proxy in front, TLS, health checks, and configuration read from the environment rather than files. These are the same whatever your API happens to do. Learn them once and every deployment after this one is faster.

One process handles one request at a time unless you run several workers. You scale up with more workers on a machine and out with more machines behind a load balancer. Calls to a language model are mostly spent waiting on the network, so concurrency helps far more here than raw processing power.

Continuous integration runs your tests on every push; continuous deployment ships whatever passes. Together they remove the manual steps people skip when they are in a hurry. Even a pipeline that only runs a linter and a build is worth setting up on the first day.

API keys belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in the repository. Rotate them on a schedule, use a different key per environment, and make certain they cannot end up in logs. A leaked provider key is billed to you until somebody notices.

When you change a prompt, a model or a retrieval setting, record what you changed and what it scored. Memory and scattered notebooks stop being sufficient the moment there are more than a handful of variants. Tools such as MLflow exist to make that record the default rather than an act of discipline.

A registry is the record of which version is approved, what it was evaluated against, and what is currently live. It is how you answer “what is in production right now” and how you roll back without guesswork. It applies to prompt and configuration versions every bit as much as to trained models.

Evaluation means scoring output against known-good examples rather than reading a few and forming an impression. Decide what correct means for your task, assemble a fixed test set, and re-run it on every change. Anything you cannot measure, you cannot safely improve.

Generated text usually has no single right answer, so evaluation combines several checks: does it contain the required facts, does it hold the format, does another model judge it acceptable, does a human sample agree. For agents you also score the steps taken, not just the final reply. Expect to build this rather than install it.

Logs are the timestamped record of what happened. For AI systems that means logging the prompt, the model, the parameters and the response — without them, a bad answer is impossible to investigate afterwards. Be deliberate about redacting anything personal before it is written down.

Metrics are numbers over time: requests per minute, error rate, latency, tokens consumed, cost. They tell you that something is wrong and roughly where to look. Watch the 95th percentile rather than the average, because averages hide exactly the slow requests users complain about.

A trace follows a single request through every step — retrieval, each model call, each tool — with timings for each. When a response takes nine seconds, the trace is what tells you which part took eight of them. This becomes essential with RAG and agents, where one request fans out into many calls.

Monitoring is collecting the signals; alerting is being told when one crosses a threshold. Alert only on things a person must act on — error spikes, latency, budget — or people learn to ignore alerts entirely. The aim is to hear about a failure before your users report it.

Kubernetes runs containers across a fleet of machines, restarting and rescheduling them as needed. It solves real problems at scale and adds substantial complexity underneath you. Understand what it does and why teams adopt it, but do not reach for it until something simpler has actually stopped being enough.

stages.title: Certification checkpoint
stages.overview: A certification will not get you hired on its own, but it supplies a syllabus and a deadline when self-directed study has stalled. The credential here covers generative AI engineering end to end, which overlaps most of stages 1 to 5. Take it whenever it is useful rather than treating it as a gate.
stages.note: Certification checkpoints are not tied to a level — take one whenever it is useful. `level` is set to mid only so the stage groups sensibly in the UI.

stages.title: Senior → AI System Architect
stages.overview: At this level the interesting questions are trade-offs rather than techniques: what quality is actually required, what it costs per request to reach it, and what you are prepared to give up. Generative systems make this sharper than most, because quality is subjective and the bill is not. The output shifts from code to design documents and the reasoning behind them.
stages.note: One architect track sits above all seven paths — the job becomes system-level judgement rather than language or framework specifics. See the career ladder.

topics.term: Model and provider selection across the whole system
topics.definition: Different parts of a system justify different models, and the choice turns on cost, latency, data residency, licensing and how much you want to depend on one vendor. Making it once for the organisation, with the reasoning written down, saves every team re-litigating it. It also means you can move when the market shifts, which it does.

Deciding in advance what the system must handle and what it is allowed to cost turns architecture into a set of constraints rather than a matter of taste. Cost per request multiplied by projected volume is the number that decides whether a design is viable at all. Set the ceiling before building, because retrofitting one means redesigning.

Somebody has to own what happens when the system is confidently wrong, leaks data, or simply stops. That means defined approval paths, audit trails, retention rules, and a named owner for each. It is unglamorous, and it is what allows AI systems to be used for anything that matters.

topics.term: Design docs and decision records over code
topics.definition: At this level the durable output is a written argument: the problem, the options considered, the choice, and why. A decision record tells whoever arrives in two years why the system is shaped this way, which is the difference between maintaining it and rewriting it. Writing clearly becomes a core technical skill rather than a soft one.

topics.term: Tying AI investment to business value
topics.definition: Every system needs an answer to what it is worth — time saved, revenue enabled, risk reduced — measured against what it costs to run. Without that, AI spend is a line item that gets cut in the first difficult quarter. Being able to make the argument is what makes this a business role as much as a technical one.
